prize_parts.citation: For the development of reversible-terminator sequencing-by-synthesis chemistry and clustered single-molecule arrays for massively parallel DNA sequencing

statement.case_for: I drop base editing and propose B012 alone. The chair asked whether the committee would accept the two-part prize or prefer sequencing alone, and the round-1 record answers it: Zou ranks B031 seventh and prefers waiting, Aqvist would hold it until the clinical record is longer, and nobody besides me defends it as a second part. I also cannot answer the Nishida and Kondo precedent with a Liu-only citation without wording that narrows it to the engineered, defined-outcome editor, and that narrowness is a weakness in a prize citation. A weak second part dilutes a strong first one, so I withdraw it. B012 stands on measurements: a 3'-O-blocked, fluorescently labelled nucleotide that a engineered polymerase incorporates and that can be cleanly unblocked on a surface, giving single-base resolution cycle after cycle, combined with single-molecule arrays that made the cost of a genome fall by several orders of magnitude. It has been independently reproduced for fifteen years, it is the substrate of almost every cancer, population-genetics and genome-stability study, and the decisive step is nucleotide chemistry, not instrumentation. Attribution to Balasubramanian and Klenerman is the cut I can defend on chemistry: they carried the reversible-terminator concept and the single-molecule array from first demonstration to the Solexa platform. It is the only mature, chemically specific, two-name configuration I see that has no prior-prize overlap.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection stands. The committee may regard sequencing as genomics technology, and Medicine could claim it. Mayer's clustering, Ju's terminators and Rothberg's pyrosequencing platform are parallel lineages that a two-name citation leaves out, and Linke ranks B012 last of his eight. Opening support is thin: only two members rank it in the top four, and the chair finds no configuration near five votes, mine included. I am also the member whose own work depends on sequencing and nucleotide measurements, so my confidence in its centrality needs to be discounted. If the committee concludes that the pool of mature, well-attributed discoveries is better represented by lipid nanoparticles or perovskites, my configuration is the one I would give up.

responses.point: Aili prefers B045 with Cullis and Langer, citing demonstrated clinical consequence, replication by many groups and a molecular-design mechanism, and treats B012 as a mature alternative.
responses.response: I agree with you on maturity and chemical specificity, and B045 is now my first alternative, which I said in no earlier round. My difficulty remains credit. Cullis, Hope and Madden hold the ionizable-lipid and rapid-mixing formulation, and Anderson and Langer hold the lipidoid and combinatorial discovery, and your pair mixes the two strands. Sparr's trio gives a cleaner chemical story but drops Langer, whom you regard as essential. Until the committee decides which strand is decisive I cannot move B045 above a discovery with a two-name cut, but if it chooses one strand I would support it.

responses.point: Zou argues B016 is the configuration most likely to survive scrutiny: a clean Miyasaka, Park, Snaith chain, replication worldwide and a structural explanation of defect tolerance, and sees stability and lead as secondary to the discovery of the absorber.
responses.response: This is the best-argued case for B016 and I accept the replication point: the efficiency numbers have been reproduced across many laboratories. Where I differ is the mechanism. You yourself say the debate on ion migration, phase segregation and grain boundaries is contested, which is the kind of unresolved measurement I would want settled before ranking above mature work. I would not block the trio, because agreement among four openings on the same three names is unusual, but my vote would stay with a discovery whose mechanism is no longer disputed. I also agree with you that B031 is too early to carry a prize, and I have dropped it.

responses.point: Linke ranks B012 last because he doubts the chemistry versus medicine fit and the competing platform lineages, and prefers B016 where the chain of credit is clearest.
responses.response: I take the lineage concern seriously, and it is why I keep the credit to Balasubramanian and Klenerman. Reversible termination is the chemical idea, and the clustering and platform work that Mayer, Ju and Rothberg did was parallel. On fit, the decisive step is the design of a polymerase-compatible, cleavable nucleotide, which Physiology or Medicine is unlikely to recognise as its own. On your point that perovskite credit is clearest, I disagree: Gratzel, Seok and Kanatzidis are acknowledged as credible by four of you, and dye-cell priority is blurred, so B016 is not cleaner than a two-name sequencing citation.

responses.point: Somfai holds B043 to be mainly a design principle for heterobifunctional molecules, with no approved PROTAC drug and a credit split between Crews, Deshaies and Handa, Ito; he holds B012 as an alternative.
responses.response: Your point on credit is the reason B043 stays an alternative. Crews and Deshaies hold the PROTAC concept, and Handa, Ito and Ciulli hold the cereblon and VHL ligand chemistry; no three names cover both without excluding someone decisive. That also answers the chair's question for me: I would not put Handa or Ciulli into a trio until the clinical record settles which line is decisive. I appreciate that you keep B012 as an alternative, and I would sooner see the committee test B012 against B052 than see either dismissed without a vote.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats sequencing-by-synthesis as chemistry rather than genomics, and whether Medicine would claim it.
Whether leaving out Mayer, Ju and Rothberg is defensible in a citation that rests on the reversible-terminator chemistry and the single-molecule array.
Whether B045 can be given a clean two- or three-name cut, in which case I would reconsider it as the lead.
Whether my own reliance on sequencing data makes me overweight B012.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have no tie to Balasubramanian, Klenerman, Mayer, Ju, Rothberg or any credited person in my alternatives, and the Umeå, Cold Spring Harbor and Rothstein networks do not include them. My own research relies on sequencing and nucleotide-pool measurements, which could bias me toward B012, and I flag that. I do not seek recusal.
